items.prompt: What is total comp?
choices: Base, bonus and equity added up for the same year
The base salary after any raise has been applied
The largest single payment received in a year
items.explanation: Total comp adds all three components over one window.

items.prompt: Dana's raise letter says +5.6%. Which part of her pay does that percentage describe?
choices: Her base salary and her bonus
Her base salary only
Her base, bonus and equity together
items.explanation: $8,000 on $142,000 is the base increase and nothing else.

items.prompt: Which of Dana's components is scheduled to fall to $0 next year?
choices: The base salary
The target bonus
The equity tranche
items.explanation: Her grant's last tranche vests this year and no new grant has been offered.

items.prompt: Dana's target bonus is 10% of a $150,000 base. How much is it?
Dana's base is $150,000, bonus $15,000 and equity $14,000. What is her total comp?
Why is a bonus called a 'target'?
choices: It is always paid in full each year
It is tied to the price of the company's shares
It is paid only if targets are hit
items.explanation: A target is the intended amount; the actual payout can be lower or zero.

items.prompt: A base-only percentage is accurate about how many of the three components?
choices: One
Two
All three
items.explanation: It speaks only about the fixed salary.

items.prompt: Which component is the fixed salary paid every period?
choices: Bonus
Base
Equity
items.explanation: Base is the steady part; bonus and equity vary.

items.prompt: Next year Dana's base and bonus stay the same and the last equity tranche ends. What is her total, and how does it change from this year's $179,000?
choices: $179,000, unchanged from this year
$165,000, down $8,000 from this year
$150,000, down $29,000 from this year
items.explanation: Base 150,000 plus bonus 15,000 is 165,000, which is 14,000 below 179,000. The drop is exactly the tranche that ends.
items.reference:
Three components, three shapes
💵 Base: fixed, paid every period
🎯 Bonus: a target, paid only if targets are hit
📈 Equity: tranches that can end at $0
Why: a percentage on base alone describes one of the three, so it cannot judge the whole package.
items.learnMore:
Total comp is base plus bonus plus equity

Each component changes differently from year to year. A base-only percentage is accurate about the fixed salary and silent about the pieces most likely to swing.

Common mistake

Treating a raise percentage as the change in total pay.

items.prompt: Dana's total rose from $170,200 to $179,000, about 5.2%, while her base rose 5.6%. What is the accurate reading?
choices: Base and total comp rose by the same number of dollars
Total comp rose, but that says nothing about next year
Total comp rose, so next year's pay is secured as well
Base rose 5.6%, so total comp must have risen 5.6%
items.explanation: Base rose $8,000 and total rose $8,800, so neither the percentages nor the dollars match. Neither number covers the year after this one.

Only A, because an $8,000 base gain is more than $3,000
Both, because both base salaries went up
Neither, because equity is not counted in pay

items.prompt: What does P50 mean in a market band?
choices: Exactly half of all comparable people earn this very amount
Pay is fifty percent above the average for the role
Half of comparable people earn less and half earn more
items.explanation: P50 is the median of the range.

items.prompt: In the unit's made-up band, where does Dana's $179,000 sit?
choices: A little above the median
Near the top, close to P90
Below the bottom of the range
items.explanation: P50 is $175,000 and P75 is $205,000, so 179,000 is just past the median.

items.prompt: Why does a number need a band to be judged?
choices: A band makes the number itself grow larger
The raw figure alone does not show how it ranks
Bands replace the need to know the role
items.explanation: Without the range you cannot say if it is low, middle or high.

items.prompt: Which percentile is the median?
items.explanation: The median splits the range in half.

items.prompt: A number at P90 means roughly what?
choices: Only about one in ten comparable people earn more
Ninety percent of pay comes from the bonus
It is ninety percent of the median
items.explanation: P90 is near the top of the range.

items.prompt: A band is useful when it covers which people?
choices: Any engineer anywhere in the world
The same role, level and location
Every employee at one company
items.explanation: A band only helps when the jobs are comparable.

items.prompt: Which sentence actually uses a band?
choices: $179,000 sounds like a very large amount of money
A friend told me she earns quite a bit more than that
$179,000 sits a little above the median for the role
items.explanation: Only the first places the number in a range.

items.prompt: In the made-up band, which value is P75?
Offer X totals $196,700 and offer Y totals $179,000. The band has P50 at $175,000 and P75 at $205,000. Which reading is right?
choices: X sits exactly at P75 and Y sits exactly at the median
Y is below the median line and X is already well above P90
X is roughly three-quarters of the way to P75; Y is just past P50
Both are above P75 because both are higher than the $175,000 median
items.explanation: X is (196,700 - 175,000) / 30,000, about 72% of the way; Y is about 13%. Neither claim about P75 or P90 holds.
items.reference:
Assumed band (made-up numbers)
P25 $150,000
P50 $175,000 (the median)
P75 $205,000
P90 $230,000
Why: a number only means something once you know where it falls in the range for the same role.
items.learnMore:
A band turns a figure into a position

A market band lists a few points on the range of comparable pay. Where a number falls tells you more than how large it sounds in isolation.

Common mistake

Judging a figure as high or low by how big it feels instead of by its place in the band.
items.reflection: Pick a number you have heard called generous. If you had the band for that role, what do you think you would find?

items.prompt: Dana's offer is judged against a band built for a different city and a different job scope. What is the likeliest result?
choices: A rank that is more accurate because the sample is larger
A precise-looking rank that compares unlike jobs
No effect, since percentiles are the same everywhere
A rank that is always too low, never too high
items.explanation: A band only means something for comparable roles. A mismatched one can err in either direction while still looking exact.

Below P25, because equity is zero
Between P50 and P75, close to P75
Between P25 and the median, below the median
items.explanation: 165,000 is above 150,000 and below 175,000. A raise this year can still leave next year below the median.

items.prompt: What is a vesting schedule?
choices: The price at which shares are first sold
A calendar that releases a grant in tranches
A list of who owns the company
items.explanation: Shares become yours tranche by tranche.

items.prompt: Unvested shares are best described as what?
choices: Cash already available to spend
A guaranteed bonus
A future promise, not current pay
items.explanation: Only vested shares are yours.

items.prompt: What is a cliff in a grant?
choices: A minimum wait before any shares vest
A sudden fall in the share price
The very last tranche of a grant
items.explanation: Leave before the cliff and you receive nothing.

items.prompt: What is a refresher grant?
choices: A refund paid out for shares that were sold early
A new grant issued before the old one runs out
A cut to the size of an existing grant at review
items.explanation: It keeps the yearly equity from dropping off an edge.

items.prompt: Dana's 4,000 RSUs vest 1,000 per year at $14 per share. What does one tranche vest for?
items.explanation: 1,000 shares times $14.

items.prompt: Without a refresher, what does Dana's fifth-year tranche vest for?
items.explanation: The original grant is fully vested after year four.

items.prompt: Why does a refresher matter to total comp?
choices: It raises the base salary automatically each year
It keeps yearly equity from dropping to zero
It guarantees the share price will keep rising
items.explanation: It fills the gap where the old schedule ends.

items.prompt: Someone leaves before a one-year cliff. What is their grant worth?
choices: A quarter of the grant
The whole grant
items.explanation: No shares vest before the cliff.

items.prompt: A new hire's grant has a one-year cliff and then vests 25% a year. She leaves after ten months. How much of the grant is hers?
choices: About 21%, prorated by months worked
25%, because one tranche was started
None, because the cliff was not reached
All of it, because it was granted on day one
items.explanation: Nothing vests before the cliff, so ten months earns nothing. Prorating only applies after vesting begins.
items.reference:
Dana's grant, year by year (assumed $14/share)
Years 1-4: $14,000 vests each year
Year 5, no refresher: $0
A refresher starts new tranches before the old ones end
Why: equity pays out on a calendar, so a one-year snapshot cannot show the year the calendar runs out.
items.learnMore:
Vesting is a calendar, not a lump sum

Unvested shares are a promise. A grant can look large on paper while paying only one tranche per year, and the tranches stop when the schedule ends unless a new grant takes over.

Common mistake

Counting the whole grant's paper value as this year's pay.
items.reflection: Think of any benefit that pays out on a schedule. What happens to your income picture in the year the schedule ends?

items.prompt: Dana's total is $179,000 this year and $165,000 next year with no refresher. Which view of her pay reveals that drop?
choices: A year-by-year look at what vests in each coming year
A comparison of this year's total to last year's total
A look at her base salary alone across several years
A comparison of her bonus percentage to the market
items.explanation: The drop is between this year and next, so a forward, multi-year view is needed. A look back at last year cannot show it.

$8,400 equity, $173,400 total

choices: The grant is taxed at a rate that removes most of it

items.prompt: What is the first step of the process?
choices: Gather data from several sources
Place the number in a band
Adjust for cost of living
items.explanation: Everything else depends on having data to work from.

items.prompt: What does it mean to normalize offers?
choices: Round every figure to the nearest thousand
Put them in the same components over the same window
Divide each one by its cost of living
items.explanation: Normalizing makes the numbers the same shape.

items.prompt: What does step 3 do?
choices: Collects several more outside sources of data
Negotiates the final offer with the employer
Finds a number's percentile in the band
items.explanation: Placing says where the number ranks.

items.prompt: Which of these belongs to step 4, adjusting for context?
choices: Cost of living and liquidity
Collecting a recruiter's range
Adding up base and bonus
items.explanation: Step 4 asks what a number is worth to you.

items.prompt: Why use more than one source?
choices: More sources always give a bigger number
No single source is reliable on its own
One source is enough if it is recent
items.explanation: Each kind of source has a typical weakness.

items.prompt: What is a typical weakness of a recruiter's stated range?
choices: It is always several years out of date by now
It can never be tied to any real open job
It is one data point with its own incentive
items.explanation: It is current, but it is a single, interested view.

items.prompt: Which comparison is badly normalized?
choices: Base pay for one offer against total comp for another
Total comp for both offers over one year
Base plus bonus plus equity for both offers
items.explanation: Mixing shapes is the exact mismatch normalizing prevents.

items.prompt: Two or three sources roughly agree. What can Dana do?
choices: Ignore all of them and rely on a friend
Lean on the band with more confidence
Pick the highest figure and use that
items.explanation: Agreement between independent sources is a good sign.

items.prompt: Dana lists base pay for one job and total comp for another, then ranks them. Which step did she skip, and what is the effect?
choices: Normalizing; the comparison mixes unlike shapes
Gathering; she has too little data to compare them
Placing in the band; she has no ranking at all
Adjusting for context; she ignored the city
items.explanation: Normalizing means the same components over the same window. Without it the ranking is meaningless even if everything else was done.
items.reference:
The four steps
1. Gather: several independent sources
2. Normalize: same components, same window
3. Place: find the percentile in the band
4. Adjust: cost of living, liquidity, one-time items
Why: each step prevents a different wrong conclusion, and skipping one leaves its failure in the result.
items.learnMore:
A process beats a single figure

A friend's number, a recruiter's range and a public table are all useful and all partial. Running them through the same four steps makes them comparable.

Common mistake

Jumping from a single anecdote straight to an ask.
items.reflection: Where else do you judge a number you were handed, such as a price or a rent? Which of the four steps do you usually skip?

items.prompt: A public source shows a median near $160,000 and a recruiter's range starts at $190,000. What is the best response?
choices: Average the two ranges and use the result as the only number
Trust the recruiter, because that range is tied to a real open job
Check the level and place match, then treat the gap as a signal
Ignore both and use the friend's figure from last month's talk
items.explanation: A big disagreement often means the sources measure different levels, places or periods. Averaging or picking one hides that.

items.prompt: Dana places a base-only number in a band built from total-comp figures. What is the likely result?
choices: The number looks higher in the band than it really is
The number lands exactly at the median either way
The band becomes more accurate for her role
The number looks lower in the band than it really is

items.prompt: A city costs more to live in. The same salary there buys what?
choices: More than it would at home
Exactly the same
Less than it would at home
items.explanation: Higher costs reduce purchasing power.

items.prompt: Assume a 1.25 cost factor. What is $196,700 worth at home?
A signing bonus is what kind of payment?
choices: An ongoing yearly payment
A one-time payment
A tax refund
items.explanation: It pays once, usually in year one.

items.prompt: Public-company RSUs can usually be sold when?
choices: Only at a future exit event
Never
Soon after they vest
items.explanation: They trade on a live market.

items.prompt: Private-company equity usually becomes cash when?
choices: At an exit event such as a sale
As soon as it is first granted to the employee
Every month, automatically, after vesting
items.explanation: That exit may be years away or never come.

items.prompt: Why leave the signing bonus out of a steady-state comparison?
choices: It is illegal to count it
It does not repeat in later years
It is always too small to matter
items.explanation: The comparison is about year-after-year pay.

items.prompt: Which equity is riskier, all else equal?
choices: Public and tradeable
They are never different
Private and illiquid
items.explanation: A private appraisal need not become real cash.

items.prompt: What does a cost-of-living index give you?
choices: An estimate of living costs
A guarantee of your expenses
The legal minimum wage
items.explanation: It is an input to a decision, not a certainty.

items.prompt: Offer X is $200,000 in a city costing 1.25 times your current one. Offer Y is $170,000 at home. Which gives more purchasing power at home?
choices: X, since it is $30,000 higher
Neither, since both are above the median
Y, since X is worth $160,000 at home
X, since cost of living only affects base pay
items.explanation: 200,000 / 1.25 = 160,000, which is below 170,000. The raw gap reverses once costs are applied.
items.reference:
What the raw number hides
🏙️ Cost of living: $196,700 / 1.25 = $157,360 (assumed factor)
💧 Liquidity: private appraisal vs public price
1️⃣ One-time items: a signing bonus pays once
Why: two equal dollar figures are not equal in value when the place, the risk or the timing differs.
items.learnMore:
Adjusting turns dollars into value

After placing a number in the band, the remaining question is what it is worth to you: what it buys where you would live, how soon it is spendable, and whether it repeats.

Common mistake

Using a cost-of-living index as a verdict instead of one input to a trade-off.
items.reflection: Imagine the same salary offered in two places with different living costs. What would you want to know beyond the index?

Appraisals are always higher than market prices
items.explanation: A private appraisal is paper value until an exit. The risk differs even when the figures match.
